opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a real possibility, but I'd be careful about the word "simply." Test-time compute is a powerful lever. We've seen that letting a model think longer, explore alternatives, check its own work, and backtrack gives big gains on hard reasoning problems. That was true in games long before language models. In poker and Go, adding search at inference time was often worth more than scaling up training by orders of magnitude. So I'm bullish on the general direction.

But research isn't one long reasoning problem. It's figuring out which questions are worth asking, running experiments, getting messy feedback from the real world, and noticing when something surprising is actually important rather than noise. Some of that is bottlenecked by wall-clock time and interaction with the environment, not just thinking. You can't think your way out of an experiment that takes a week to run.

So I'd frame it this way: more test-time compute will make models dramatically better research assistants, and then increasingly research collaborators. They'll grind through proofs, debug code, and generate and filter hypotheses at a scale no human team can match. Whether that becomes "replacing researchers" depends on progress in other areas too: longer-horizon agency, better judgment about what matters, and the ability to learn from their own experiments over time.

I wouldn't bet against it happening, and I think it could happen faster than many people expect. I just don't think it's purely a matter of turning up the inference budget. It's test-time compute plus everything around it.

r001.rationale: It says more inference compute alone will not replace researchers; progress in other areas is also needed.

r002.rationale: It describes gains from additional test-time compute and does not say models fail to improve on any benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It identifies judging which questions matter and recognizing important findings as limitations relevant to research.

r004.rationale: It says models will become dramatically better research assistants, communicating that they can help human researchers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the framing of "just add more test-time compute" undersells what's actually going on, but I also think the direction is real.

Here's how I'd break it down. What we found with reasoning models is that test-time compute is genuinely a new axis of scaling, and it's one that hasn't been exhausted the way pretraining has started to feel. If you let a model think for seconds versus minutes versus hours, you see consistent improvements on hard, verifiable problems. That's a big deal, because for a long time the entire field was organized around getting the answer out in a single forward pass.

But replacing a researcher is a different question than scoring higher on a benchmark. Research isn't one problem with a known answer that you can grind on. It's choosing which problem to work on, noticing that an experiment is giving you a weird result, deciding the original plan was wrong and pivoting. A lot of that involves taste and long-horizon judgment, and the feedback loop is noisy and slow. Math competitions and coding problems are great training grounds precisely because you can verify the outcome cheaply. Science mostly isn't like that yet.

So my honest view is: I don't think there's some magic threshold where you give a model a million dollars of compute on a prompt and it produces a Nobel-caliber result. What I do think is that the models are getting better at the pieces, and the pieces compound. Right now they're useful for accelerating a researcher, writing the code, checking a proof, exploring the space of ideas faster. The gap between "very good assistant" and "autonomous researcher" closes as we get better at letting these models operate over longer horizons and learn from less clean reward signals. That's an active research problem, not something that falls out automatically from more inference.

The thing I'd caution against is the tendency to anchor on the current failure modes. People said reasoning models wouldn't generalize outside of math and code, and that turned out to be mostly wrong. So I try to be humble about timelines. I'd be surprised if it happened next year. I'd also be surprised if, in a decade, AI wasn't doing a substantial fraction of what we currently call research.

r001.rationale: It says more inference alone will not automatically produce an autonomous researcher and describes research skills beyond benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: It says additional test-time compute improves performance on hard, verifiable problems; it does not say that some benchmarks fail to improve.

r003.rationale: It identifies taste and long-horizon judgment as parts of research that current models lack or struggle with.

r004.rationale: It says current models accelerate researchers by writing code, checking proofs, and exploring ideas faster.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but I wouldn’t assume that giving a model more test-time compute is sufficient by itself. There’s a difference between spending longer solving a well-defined problem and doing research, where part of the challenge is figuring out what question to ask and what evidence would change your mind.

For that extra compute to help, the model needs a productive way to use it: exploring different ideas, running experiments, checking results, and revising its approach. If it’s just spending more time elaborating on a mistaken assumption, you haven’t gained much.

So I’d separate two questions. Can more test-time compute make models substantially better at research tasks? I think that’s a very promising direction. Does that imply you can take a fixed model, let it run long enough, and replace a researcher? That’s a much stronger claim, and I don’t think we should take it for granted.

r001.rationale: It says more test-time compute alone should not be assumed sufficient to replace a researcher; models also need a productive way to use it.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim about benchmarks where additional test-time compute fails to improve performance.

r003.rationale: It discusses choosing research questions and evaluating evidence, but does not identify weak research taste as a limitation of current models.

r004.rationale: It does not state that using AI models makes human researchers more effective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s plausible, but I wouldn’t assume that you can take a fixed model, give it arbitrarily more time to think, and eventually get a great researcher. The question is whether it can use that additional compute productively. Can it explore different approaches, recognize when an approach has failed, and come up with something better?

Research is particularly interesting because you often don’t have an easy way to check the answer. In math, you might be able to verify a proof. In empirical research, you have to run an experiment, interpret the result, and decide what to try next. So a longer chain of thought by itself isn’t necessarily enough. You want a system that can interact with that feedback loop.

But I also wouldn’t dismiss the possibility that this gets us very far. If a model can make meaningful progress over a few minutes, and we can train it to keep making progress over hours or days, that could be a substantial change. I’d look at how performance improves as you give it more compute, rather than assume either that it hits a wall or that scaling automatically solves research.

r001.rationale: The response says that giving a fixed model arbitrarily more time does not ensure it becomes a great researcher; it must use the added compute productively and interact with research feedback.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating performance as compute increases but does not state that current models fail to improve on any benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It does not identify weak research taste as a limitation.

r004.rationale: It does not state that using AI models makes human researchers more effective.
